doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Motivating students with living players and practice logs
summary: Students bring solos by Hargrove or Harrell; his wife explains his firsthand experience with Dizzy, Miles and others. A practice log from Shawn Wallace keeps students honest.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: each particular — what got each particular student energized and motivated. And so a quick aside to that is for young people I’ve been finding, maybe you found this, that if the person is living then they’re more apt to be attracted to it. I don’t know if you’ve gotten that. So check it out. So I’ll tell somebody hey, bring — I want to have them do what they want to do first. I say, “Bring in a transcribed solo, anybody you want to, let’s work on it next week. Write it out a little bit if you can, if you can memorize it without writing it out fine but bring in something and we’ll work on that. And people would bring in Roy Hargrove and Tom Harrell and Terrell Stafford, and all people that I love, right? And I would sort of nudge them like, “Hey you know, you want to try Dizzy next time?” And it was like, but I’ve got these guys. And I talked to my wife who is very smart, and I said, “Why is that?” And she goes, “Byron, you knew Dizzy Gillespie. You met Miles Davis. You saw Roy Eldridge play a bunch of times. You didn’t see Louis. You saw and sat next to Freddie Hubbard and played with him. Just go down the list. That’s what they’re looking for.” So for some — this is not all people — and eventually they get to like, “Oh I transcribed Roy Hargrove and it sounds like Miles, maybe I need to check out Miles.” So it’s just an interesting way. So that’s what I did for motivation. But also finally is practicing. Because I had a student, you know, tell me like, yeah, he played the thing, he’s like, “Sorry I didn’t have a chance to practice.” And I’m like, “You don’t think I know that? I can hear that. I know.” I’m not like one of these guys, but I know when you haven’t practiced so just know that you can’t fake it for me. And we can just be honest with each other. And I understand there’s times when you can’t practice. So I did use an approach with a friend of mine, Shawn “Thunder” Wallace. A great sax player. He’s the head of the department at Ohio State University. And he said, “Make them keep a practice log, and log in and just have them, they need to show you that.” Now you can lie on that too, but it’s tougher. Because you’re telling me you practiced every day for an hour on this exercise and these things and that’s where you’re at? I don’t believe that. So it’s harder to lie.
It takes me back to fifth grade when you used to put down, you know, this day, and then your parents were supposed to sign it.
Right. Exactly. Exactly. Well I guess you become your own parent when you get in college so.
